name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,887

clue.text: Climber melted last ice with bit of muesli (8)

indicators.note: Ice that has melted keeps everything it was made of and none of the shape, which is what happens to these letters.
A bit chipped off a word is the letter at its front, the only piece you can take without being told where to cut.

blocks.note: seven letters handed over whole, in an order the solver has to abandon
the opening letter of the cereal supplies the eighth

explanation.walkthrough: Everything in the surface is a mountain: a climber, melting ice, breakfast before the ascent. The climber wanted is a plant on a garden wall.
explanation.definitionFit: Climber -> CLEMATIS: the general word for the particular plant, since clematis is one of the flowering climbers that haul themselves up walls and trellises.

clue.text: Fancy bishop does nothing with much passion (4,6)

blocks.note: to fancy something is to like it, the mild sense of the word
B is the bishop on a chess scoresheet, the one place the piece is routinely a letter
someone doing nothing lazes about

explanation.walkthrough: Three separate pieces sit end to end while the surface reads as one idle churchman, and the phrase they build is nothing to do with the church.
explanation.definitionFit: with much passion -> LIKE BLAZES: to work or run like blazes is to do it fiercely, at the pace of a fire, so the phrase means flat out.

clue.text: Friar spat regularly beneath cross in seminary (7)

indicators.note: Something done regularly happens at a steady interval, and letters picked at a steady interval means every second one.
This is a down entry, where beneath means lower in the grid, so the letters picked here are written after the ones clued next.

blocks.note: cross in the sense of angry, not the Christian symbol the surface wants
the even-numbered letters of the two words, counting from the second

explanation.walkthrough: Friar, cross and seminary all point at a Christian house of study, and the school being defined is an Islamic one, where the Koran and religious law are taught.
explanation.definitionFit: seminary -> MADRASA: a madrasa is the Muslim school of religious instruction, so it is a seminary in the plain sense of a college training clergy.

clue.text: Did flirt ruffle Daisy's skirts with toe? (5)

indicators.note: Ruffled cloth no longer lies flat, and letters that have been ruffled no longer lie in the order they were given.
To skirt something is to go round its edge, so what is kept of the name is the letter at each end and nothing between.

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the name, the pair that edge it
three letters handed over intact, to be jumbled with the other two

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a saucy scene at a garden party, complete with a ruffled skirt. Daisy is a name to be dismantled rather than a woman being bothered.
explanation.definitionFit: Did flirt -> TOYED: to toy with someone is to flirt without meaning any of it, and the past tense matches the clue's word for word.

clue.text: Relative keeps walking (7)

blocks.note: walking is a business of steps, one to a pace
to keep doing a thing is to go on doing it, and this little word carries that continuing

explanation.walkthrough: Two words that describe someone still trudging along the road, run together, name a member of the family instead. The whole trick is where you put the gap.
explanation.definitionFit: Relative -> STEPSON: he is family through a parent's remarriage rather than by blood, which is exactly the loose reach the word relative has.

clue.text: That woman sounded doubly pretentious (6)

indicators.note: What is described here is heard, not spelt, so you write down a word that merely matches the noise.
The little word you hear is not used once but twice over, back to back, which is where the length comes from.

blocks.note: the pronoun that stands in for a female person
say that pronoun twice and the sound is spelt this way in the word English took from French

explanation.walkthrough: The pronoun does not contribute a single letter of its own spelling; only the noise it makes survives, and French spelling supplies the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: pretentious -> CHICHI: borrowed from French for the fussily stylish, the showy smartness of someone trying visibly too hard.

clue.text: Cold tea left in canteen (9)

indicators.note: A thing said to be in another is written inside it, so the single letter named just before drops between the letters of the word that follows.

blocks.note: char is the British word for a cup of tea
L is the standard abbreviation for left
the mess is the canteen soldiers eat in, and it splits to take the letter above

explanation.walkthrough: Cold tea left in a canteen is one miserable picture and none of it is the definition: cold here is said of a person, and the tea is a separate piece of the build.
explanation.definitionFit: Cold -> CHARMLESS: of a manner rather than a temperature, cold means unwelcoming, and a charmless person offers exactly that much warmth.

clue.text: Profound how decimal system counts irrational number (7)

blocks.note: a decimal system counts in tens, and the phrase is taken at its word
e is the mathematician's constant, 2.718..., irrational like pi and written as one letter

explanation.walkthrough: The irrational number a solver reaches for first is pi. The one that fits is its neighbour from the same maths, and it is only ever one letter long.
explanation.definitionFit: Profound -> INTENSE: of feeling rather than thought, where profound grief and intense grief name the same depth of emotion.

clue.text: Worker delivered new parts (4)

indicators.note: When something parts it opens down the middle, and the letter named just before it steps into the gap.

blocks.note: a mother who delivered a baby had it, the everyday way of saying she gave birth
N is the standard abbreviation for new

explanation.walkthrough: Read straight, this is a mechanic's invoice. Each of the last three words is doing a different job: one is a word to be split, one a letter, one an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Worker -> HAND: the crossword's standing sense of a hired labourer on a farm or a ship, the one counted in all hands on deck.

clue.text: Small child having very weak grip (6)

blocks.note: S is small on any clothing label
kiddy is the nursery word for a young child

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a toddler with a feeble grasp. The definition belongs to roads and tyres, where grip is the friction that keeps a car pointing straight.
explanation.definitionFit: having very weak grip -> SKIDDY: said of a road surface or a tyre that lets a vehicle slide, grip being the motoring word for the hold it should have.

clue.text: Difficult pretending to be someone else on X (8)

indicators.note: In an across entry a piece laid on another comes after it, so the letters named before this word finish up at the back.

blocks.note: the letter written out the way it is said
playing a part you are not is acting

explanation.walkthrough: X is the social network, and the impostor on it is what holds the sentence together. The wordplay only wants the letter's name, said aloud as two.
explanation.definitionFit: Difficult -> EXACTING: an exacting job demands a great deal of whoever does it, which is the demanding sort of difficult rather than the puzzling sort.

clue.text: Guys that are fairly dull last to expect flattery (12)

indicators.note: Only the letter at the end of the following word is wanted, the one that comes last when you spell it out.

blocks.note: bland is dull, and the -ish on the end is what makes it only fairly so
guys are men in everyday speech
the final letter of the verb

explanation.walkthrough: The -ish suffix is the piece worth keeping: setters attach it to an adjective to mean 'roughly', and it buys them eight letters that look like a description.
explanation.definitionFit: flattery -> BLANDISHMENT: the noun for coaxing praise laid on to win somebody round, which is flattery with a purpose behind it.

clue.text: Driving fan parking here at old ground (10)

indicators.note: This is the past tense of grind, and whatever has been through a mill comes out in pieces that no longer sit where they did.

blocks.note: P is the letter on every parking sign
nine letters, which with the one above them is the full count

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ground' wants to be the field the old cars are parked on, and it is the past tense of grind instead. Nothing in the clue is a place.
explanation.definitionFit: Driving fan -> PETROLHEAD: British slang for someone besotted with cars and the driving of them, named after the fuel rather than the wheel.

clue.text: Fuel with nasty smell brought round by soldier (8)

indicators.note: Bringing a thing round turns it to face the other way, so that piece is read from its last letter back to its first.

blocks.note: a para is a paratrooper, the soldier who arrives by parachute
a niff is British slang for a bad smell, and it arrives back to front

explanation.walkthrough: The fuel really does smell, so the opening words read as one complaint and nothing marks where the definition stops. Only the first word is defining anything.
explanation.definitionFit: Fuel -> PARAFFIN: the oil burnt in lamps, stoves and heaters, and the British name for what is sold elsewhere as kerosene.

clue.text: Throwing couple of rights, initially fear punch-up (9)

indicators.note: Throwing a thing away is getting rid of it, so the letters named next are discarded rather than used.

blocks.note: initially is FIRST, and that word minus its R leaves these four letters
fear is FRIGHT, and that word minus its R leaves these five
right is R in the usual abbreviation, and two of them are what gets thrown out

explanation.walkthrough: The boxing surface earns its keep: rights are punches thrown in the ring, and here they are two letter Rs thrown out of two perfectly ordinary words.
explanation.definitionFit: punch-up -> FISTFIGHT: British for a brawl, and a fight conducted with bare hands rather than weapons is precisely that.

clue.text: Team with Pele but no wingers, well-balanced? (6)

indicators.note: A winger plays out at the edge of the pitch, so losing them takes the outermost letter off each end of the name.

blocks.note: strip a letter off each end of the footballer's name and this pair is what is left standing
an even spread is a well-balanced one

explanation.walkthrough: Pele supplies both halves of the joke: the greatest of footballers hands over two letters, and his own game is where wingers stand on the edges.
explanation.definitionFit: Team -> ELEVEN: a football or cricket side puts eleven players out, so the number is used as the name of the side itself.

clue.text: Mike wears heels for endurance race (2,4)

indicators.note: You are inside whatever you wear, so the letter doing the wearing goes into the middle of the word that follows.

blocks.note: a boat heels over, which is to say it leans
Mike is M in the radio alphabet, alongside Alpha and Bravo

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a man in high heels, and the heels wanted are a yacht's. Mike is nobody: it is the radio operator's way of saying a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: endurance race -> LE MANS: the French town whose twenty-four-hour motor race is the classic test of stamina, so its name stands for the event.

clue.text: Very keen on Gordian knots (7)

indicators.note: Knotted rope loops back through itself and comes out in no sensible order, which is what these letters do.

blocks.note: seven letters, exactly the count the clue asks for

explanation.walkthrough: The Gordian knot is the one Alexander the Great gave up untying and cut through instead, which is fair warning that these letters will not come apart tidily.
explanation.definitionFit: Very keen on -> ADORING: to adore someone is to be devoted to them, so an adoring look is the face of being extremely keen.

clue.text: One entertained by revolting celebrities on flight (8)

indicators.note: To entertain a guest is to have them in the house, so whoever is entertained goes inside the word that follows.

blocks.note: a population in revolt is said to be up, as in up in arms
the Roman numeral for one, the crossword's usual single-letter one
celebrities are stars, the film-and-television sense, and they open up to take the guest

explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolting' looks like the setter calling the celebrities disgusting, which is the wrong sense: a people in revolt are up, and that gives the first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: on flight -> UPSTAIRS: on a flight you are up in the air, which flyers call upstairs, and the same word covers being up a flight of stairs.

clue.text: Bear short of energy (7)

blocks.note: under ten is short of ten, the plain arithmetic sense
go means energy or drive, as in someone full of go

explanation.walkthrough: Go meaning energy is the piece worth pocketing: it turns up constantly, and here it hides behind a phrase that reads as one idea, running out of steam.
explanation.definitionFit: Bear -> UNDERGO: bear in the sense of endure, since you bear an operation exactly as you undergo one, putting up with what is done to you.

clue.text: Traveller first to arrive by way of height? (7)

indicators.note: Only the opening letter of the following word is wanted, the one you come to before any other.

blocks.note: the letter the verb starts with
via is the Latin for by way of, and English uses it unchanged
a tor is a rocky hilltop, the word used for the granite outcrops on Dartmoor

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark covers two loose joints at once: a tor is only one kind of height, and a flier only one kind of traveller.
explanation.definitionFit: Traveller -> AVIATOR: the general word standing for a particular case, since an aviator travels by air, and the question mark owns up to the looseness.

clue.text: Move lad with infection that mustn't be passed on (12)

indicators.note: To move a thing is to change where it sits, and what changes places here are the letters of the two words after it.

blocks.note: three letters, handed over as they stand
the other nine, and twelve is the count the clue wants

explanation.walkthrough: The surface and the definition tell the same story from different ends: a boy is shifted because he is catching, and the answer is the thing that must not be caught by anyone else.
explanation.definitionFit: that mustn't be passed on -> CONFIDENTIAL: information given in confidence is to be kept to yourself, so repeating it is the single thing forbidden.

clue.text: Hospital in south coast resort attracting particular clientele (5)

indicators.note: A thing said to be in another is written inside it, so the letter named first is planted in the middle of the town.

blocks.note: H is hospital on a road sign or a map
Nice sits on the Mediterranean coast of France, the resort town of the Riviera

explanation.walkthrough: A south coast resort sounds like Brighton or Bognor, and the coast in question is French. The word for it is spelt like an English adjective and said nothing like one.
explanation.definitionFit: attracting particular clientele -> NICHE: a niche business aims at one small, specific set of customers instead of the general public.

clue.text: Heavy blow toppled English prisoner (4)

indicators.note: Something toppled has gone over on its head, which is this setter's loose way of saying the pieces are read the other way round.

blocks.note: an old lag is British slang for a convict, and it arrives here reversed
E is the standard abbreviation for English

explanation.walkthrough: A heavy blow sounds like a punch, and the blow here is the weather's: sailors call a spell of hard wind a blow.
explanation.definitionFit: Heavy blow -> GALE: a gale is a wind strong enough to be named on the Beaufort scale, heavy being a measure of its force.

clue.text: Most of Mean Girls cast act poorly (8)

indicators.note: Most is nearly all, so what you take is everything except the very last letter.
To cast is to throw, and letters thrown down land in a heap rather than in the order they left your hand.

blocks.note: the film's title less its final letter leaves eight, the length wanted

explanation.walkthrough: 'Act poorly' reads as a review of the cast, and poorly is British for unwell: the definition is putting on an illness, not putting on a bad performance.
explanation.definitionFit: act poorly -> MALINGER: to malinger is to feign sickness to dodge work, and since poorly means ill in British usage the phrase means act ill.

clue.text: Conservative, say, one reducing spending? (6)

blocks.note: C is how the Conservative party is printed on a British ballot paper
to say something is to utter it

explanation.walkthrough: The comma after the party invites you to read 'say' as 'for example'. It is a verb here, the plain word for speak, and the commas are surface punctuation.
explanation.definitionFit: one reducing spending -> CUTTER: somebody who cuts is a cutter, and the cuts meant are the ones a chancellor makes to a budget.

clue.text: Force directed towards Earth pause when told (6)

indicators.note: Told means spoken, so what gets written down is only what the word beside it sounds like, never how that word is spelt.

blocks.note: a pause is a wait, and said aloud that word is spelt the heavier way

explanation.walkthrough: The physics is exact rather than decorative: what a scale reads is the pull of gravity on a mass, which is why the same body records less on the Moon.
explanation.definitionFit: Force directed towards Earth -> WEIGHT: in physics weight is precisely the gravitational force pulling a body downwards, as distinct from the mass being pulled.

clue.text: Emergency control on the other side of bike? (8)

blocks.note: over the road means on the far side of it
a bike is a thing you ride, and a ride is a machine you get on

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is doing real work: a bike is one ride among many, so the setter is offering an example where a synonym would not quite hold.
explanation.definitionFit: Emergency control -> OVERRIDE: the manual override is the switch that snatches control back from an automatic system when something goes wrong.
